content: Ambazone is an oral antiseptic agent. It was patented in 1957 by Bayer under the trade name Iversal and was briefly utilized in Germany. Currently, it remains in use in Russia, countries of the former Soviet Union, and Romania. However, it has not been approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The production of pharmaceutical-grade ambazone is challenging due to the presence of significant amounts of byproducts, synthetic intermediates, and decomposition products. Ambazone exhibits bacteriostatic activity against hemolytic streptococcus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and viridans streptococcus. Experimental studies have demonstrated that ambazone possesses antiseptic properties and, intriguingly, anti-tumor properties as well. The compound is prepared through solid-based crystallization or grinding methods. The mode of action of ambazone has been extensively studied. It has been shown to act through various mechanisms. Intravenous doses of up to 10^-5 mol/kg and oral doses of up to 10^-3 mol/kg have been tested. However, oral administration presents a significant limitation, as studies indicate an absorption rate of only 35-50% in one experiment and 40% in the intestines in another. This low absorption rate suggests that ambazone may not be the most effective choice for treatment, as higher concentrations would need to be ingested to achieve a therapeutic effect. The issue with higher concentrations is compounded by ambazone's half-life of 6–7 hours. Ambazone does not exhibit central nervous system (CNS) side effects, as it does not cross the blood-brain barrier. While this is a protective mechanism of the body to prevent unwanted substances from affecting the brain, it also limits the potential use of ambazone in treating brain tumors. Therapeutic studies in laboratory rats have determined the effective dose of ambazone to be 60–125 mg/kg of body weight. Its antiseptic properties are evident in its increased activity against gram-positive cocci. Additionally, ambazone has demonstrated efficacy in combating certain forms of leukemia in laboratory rats. When administered orally, it has been shown to prolong life expectancy and cure L1210 and P388 leukemia in these animal models. Researchers employed various methods to evaluate these outcomes, including mean survival time (MST), percentage increase in lifespan, survival rates, percentage changes in body weight, and the number of peritoneal cells. The results indicate significant progress in leukemia treatment. When ambazone was tested using the Ames test without metabolic activation, no mutagenic or carcinogenic properties were observed. However, when the same test was conducted with metabolic activation or when the C-Test was performed, the potential for mutagenicity was detected. These findings present two divergent outcomes, and further testing is required to determine whether the benefits of using ambazone for treatment outweigh the potential risks.
